newsitem.title: UK: Britain hints at proportional system for Euro vote.
newsitem.headline: Britain hints at proportional system for Euro vote.

text.p: Britain will use proportional representation (PR) to elect its European Parliament members in 1999, coming into line with the 14 other European Union states, an aide to Prime Minister Tony Blair indicated on Wednesday.

The Times newspaper said Blair had decided to introduce a parliamentary bill in the autumn to end the first-past-the-post system which gave his Labour Party 62 of mainland Britain's 84 seats in the Strasbourg assembly at the last elections in 1994.
"The speculation on that has been relatively accurate," the aide said, adding that the subject would be discussed at a cabinet meeting on Thursday.

But he said this did not mean that Blair had been converted to a PR system for electing the British parliament, in which he currently enjoys a 179-seat majority after a May election in which Labour received about 45 percent of the vote.

"What people should not do is imagine that this shows anything about PR for Westminster," the aide said. "The prime minister has long agreed with the view that it (PR) is far more apposite to the Strasbourg assembly."

Other EU states have long protested that the composition of the European Parliament has been distorted by the British delegation, which has ranged from 63 Conservatives and 14 Labour members in 1979 to 62 Labour and 18 Conservatives currently.
The three Northern Irish members in the European Parliament are already elected by proportional representation, ensuring representation for the minority Roman Catholic community.
But Britain's minority Liberal Democrats won their first seats in the European Parliament in 1994, gaining two after polling 16 percent of the votes.
PR would have awarded them about 10 more seats, giving them the biggest national delegation in the European Liberal Democratic group.
In a pre-election accord on constitutional reform, Labour and the Liberal Democrats agreed there should be a referendum on whether Britain should elect its parliament by a PR system.
Blair's aide declined to speculate when a commission would be appointed to prepare for this plebiscite.
